newsitem.title: INDIA: India says no debt talks for now with Russia.
newsitem.headline: India says no debt talks for now with Russia.

text.p: India said on Tuesday that it was not negotiating with Russia on converting its debt into hard currency .
"At the moment there are no talks between India and Russia over the conversion of the debt into hard currency," an Indian Finance Ministry spokeswoman told Reuters in New Delhi.
India owes Russia close to $8 billion, down from $10 billion in 1992, largely as payments for warplanes and other arms supplies, and steel products during the cold war era.

On Monday a Russian Finance Ministry official said in Moscow the two countries were holding talks on converting India's debt into hard currency. The move was aimed at increasing Russia's revenues from payments, the official said.
A Russian Embassy spokesman in New Delhi said Russia wanted all its debtors to repay in hard currency but there were no specific negotiations with India on the subject.

"Ever since Anatoly Chubais took over as the Deputy Prime Minister he has been pressing for the payment of debts in hard currency and it is part of that drive...there is nothing specific about debt from India," the spokesman said.
He added that the issue might be discussed when Chubais, who is also Russia's finance minister and the architect of the post-communist privatisation programme, visits India later this year.
"Chubais might lead a delegation to India sometime in September or October, and the whole issue might be discussed at length," the spokesman added.
India is one of Russia's biggest debtors along with Iraq, Libya and Cuba. Unlike many others, it regularly makes payments in accordance with original contracts.
But payments are in rupees, which are later sold by Russia's state-owned Vneshekonombank at a discount.

During the Cold War, India enjoyed a special trade facility which allowed it to use the rupee -- not a "hard", or convertible, currency -- to pay for Soviet goods. The Soviet Union was India's main arms supplier and steel partner.

In 1992, Russian President Boris Yeltsin visited India and signed an agreement which required India to repay $10 billion in the form of goods worth $1 billion every year over the next 12 years. But things have not gone according to plan, and Russia has never managed to purchase $1 billion worth of goods each year.
"Russia has bought goods worth about $2 billion in the last five years," M.S. Lakshmi, a Russia expert at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT) said.
Sanjeev Reddy, director general of the IIFT, said India's balance of payments could enable the country to make part payment in hard currency but that would be detrimental to its exports.
"If we repay Russia in hard currency we might hamper our own export prospects as the Russians might buy what they do from India from other countries," said Reddy.
